A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the SSFR of galaxies at high redshift is not a function of the halo mass alone, but is a function of the star formation mode.
the SSFR–M* relation at high redshift is the result of two modes of star forming galaxies, where one mode is driven by major mergers, and the other mode is driven by cold gas accretion.
the observed high SSFR at z≳4 can be explained by the combination of two modes: mode 1 (merger-triggered star formation) and mode 2 (cold accretion-regulation).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the star formation history and the SSFR–stellar relation are sensitive to the star formation efficiency during galaxy mergers, which can be used to constrain the physical processes during mergers.
star formation in galaxies is not a continuous process, and that star forming galaxies can have very different star formation efficiencies depending on their environment.

the observed high SSFRs of low-mass high redshift galaxies are not in conflict with the observed low SSFR of low mass low redshift galaxies, but are a natural outcome from the different modes of star formation in high and low redshift galaxies.
